comments.text:
In biological research, a gain-of-function (GoF) mutation is a genetic alteration that gives an organism, cell, or protein a new biological ability or enhances an existing one. This contrasts with a loss-of-function mutation, which disables or reduces a trait.
While GoF mutations occur constantly in nature through evolution, "gain-of-function research" usually refers to scientists intentionally inducing these mutations in a laboratory to study how organisms adapt, predict future threats, or develop new medical and agricultural technologies.
Here is how this research is applied across different fields of biology:
1. Virology and Epidemiology
In virology, researchers alter pathogens to understand how they might naturally evolve to become more dangerous. This is known as "Dual-Use Research of Concern" because the findings are highly valuable for public health (like designing vaccines), but carry biosafety risks if a modified pathogen were to escape the lab.
 * The H5N1 Avian Flu Studies (2011): The H5N1 bird flu is highly lethal to humans but naturally does not spread easily from person to person. Two separate research teams genetically modified the virus to see what it would take for it to become airborne among mammals. By repeatedly passing the virus through ferrets, they discovered that only a handful of specific mutations were needed for the virus to spread via respiratory droplets.
 * The Goal: This was done to warn global health organizations about exactly which natural mutations to look out for in wild bird populations, and to begin designing targeted stockpiles of vaccines before a potential pandemic could start.
2. Oncology (Cancer Research)
Cancer is fundamentally driven by natural gain-of-function mutations in human cells. Researchers study these mutations extensively to figure out how to stop hyperactive cell growth.
 * The RAS Oncogene: Normal RAS genes act as temporary on/off switches for cell division. A GoF mutation in these genes can lock the resulting protein in the "on" position, telling the cell to divide continuously, which leads to tumor growth.
 * The Goal: By deliberately recreating these GoF mutations in laboratory cell cultures or animal models, scientists can test experimental targeted therapies to see if they can successfully "turn off" or bypass the hyperactive protein.
3. Agriculture and Biotechnology
In agricultural science, GoF research is used to create crops that can survive harsh conditions or resist pests, directly altering the global food supply chain.
 * Pest and Drought Resistance: Scientists have introduced genes into crops like corn and cotton that give the plants the new function of producing a harmless-to-humans protein that is toxic to specific insect pests (such as Bt corn). Similarly, researchers induce mutations to upregulate certain plant proteins that help crops retain water more efficiently in arid environments.
 * The Goal: To increase crop yields, drastically reduce the need for chemical pesticide sprays, and prepare agriculture for shifting climate conditions.

I think the early COVID mandates are usefully compared to the blackout regulations imposed during World War II.

During an air raid or submarine threat, people were required to turn off or cover their lights. The government was not claiming that one uncovered window would necessarily cause a bombing or sink a ship. The point was that visible lights collectively made everyone more vulnerable. On the American coast, illuminated cities could silhouette merchant ships for German U-boats. Some coastal communities initially resisted blackouts because businesses feared losing tourism, but the continued lights made enemy targeting easier.
The moral logic was simple: your light may belong to you, but the danger it creates does not stop at your property line.

The same principle applied during the opening stages of COVID. An infectious person could endanger strangers without realizing it. Evidence of presymptomatic and asymptomatic transmission was still emerging in the spring of 2020, meaning that people who felt perfectly healthy could nevertheless spread the virus. Masks, distancing, limits on crowded gatherings, temporary closures, and isolation rules were attempts to reduce that shared danger while scientists learned how the virus spread, how deadly it was, which populations were most vulnerable, and what measures actually worked. All while confronting supply shortages and the Administration's attempt to pit Red states against Blue states in bidding to see who could get the last crate of horse pills. 

That does not mean every rule was perfectly designed, consistently communicated, or kept in place for precisely the right length of time. Wartime governments also made mistakes, overreacted in some areas, acted too slowly in others, and sometimes allowed fear or prejudice to produce terrible abuses. Emergency powers should always be questioned, reviewed, and withdrawn when they are no longer necessary.

But uncertainty itself was not an argument for doing nothing. It was the reason precautions were necessary. When a threat may be catastrophic, waiting for complete knowledge can mean waiting until prevention is no longer possible.

This is why I regard Dr. Fauci’s service during the pandemic as heroic - not because he was infallible or because he personally dictated every policy, but because he accepted the responsibility of advising the country during a rapidly developing emergency. He had to interpret incomplete evidence in public, revise recommendations as scientists learned more, and do so while political leaders and media figures were telling us to drink bleach, shove lights up our asses, while turning basic public-health questions into tests of partisan loyalty. 

Changing advice in response to new evidence is not proof that Dr. Fauci failed. It is what responsible science looks like when knowledge is being produced in real time.

A blackout only worked when people understood that extinguishing their own light was not an act of submission. It was an act of solidarity. The early pandemic precautions asked something similar of us: accept a temporary inconvenience because your behavior could expose someone else to a danger they had no meaningful way to avoid.

The central question was never merely, “What risks am I personally willing to take?” It was also, “What risks do I have the right to impose on everyone around me?”
